newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bonn to sell Telekom shares.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonn to sell Telekom shares.

text.p: Deutsche Telekom AG, the German telecoms giant, said on Thursday it has reached an agreement with the government allowing Bonn to sell some of its remaining shares to boost its bid for European monetary union.

The government will transfer a package of shares equivalent to 25 percent of Telekom's capital to the state development agency Kreditanstalt fuer Wiederaufbau (KfW) in two steps in 1997 and 1998 and sell them later to strategic investors.

German government sources have said that the sale could raise as much as 25 billion marks ($14.5 billion) over the next two years, but it is unclear whether the government will be able to apply this in its attempt to meet the fiscal targets for monetary union.
Deutsche Telekom shares opened down 1.36 percent at 42.20 marks in computerised IBIS trade. Shares edged back up and rose above Wednesday's IBIS close of 42.78 marks in early business.
While it remains unclear how the sale will help the government qualify for European economic and monetary union, the sale could have a clearly positive impact on Telekom.

"In this way the government will dispose of its majority stake in Deutsche Telekom sooner than planned, increasing the company's flexibility in order to develop into a global player on the world market," Telekom chairman Ron Sommer said in a statement ahead of the company's annual shareholders meeting.

The deal also allows Telekom to search for strategic investors for some of the shares the government plans to sell and the company said it was satisfied that the deal was in the best interests of all of its shareholders.

"As strategic investors, we are looking at current and future partners in the international telecommunications business," Sommer said, declining to say which potential investors the company was considering.
The government still holds a 74-percent stake in Deutsche Telekom after 26 percent was sold to the public in November.

Industry analysts have considered an equity swap between Deutsche Telekom and France Telecom possible in order to anchor their strategic alliance, but the company has given few indications since its 1996 flotation about its plans.
The German and French telecoms groups together own 20 percent of U.S. long-distance carrier Sprint Corp and the three companies operate the Global One corporate telecommunications venture.
Deutsche Telekom has held talks with Cable and Wireless Plc about a link between the British-based telecoms group and Global One and it has sought a strategic partner in Asia.

Sommer said the government's sale of additional shares would not hurt the company's two million private shareholders who bought stock in its $13 billion listing last year, saying none of shares would be sold on capital markets before 2000.

In the run up to Deutsche Telekom's partial privatisation, Bonn indicated it would not dispose of its shares before the year 2000. The law privatising Telekom states that none of the shares can be sold directly on the market before then, but allows for private placements.

But with Bonn finding it difficult to rein in its deficit in time to qualify for EMU, Finance Minister Theo Waigel recently said he intended to step up all privatisations and to dispose of Telekom shares early.
The daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung newspaper said on Thursday that the deal would raise 10 billion marks for Bonn this year and another 15 billion next year.

Telekom said that the government's plan to sell its shares would not affect the company's option to carry out the second half of its approved capital increase, which has a remaining volume of 287 million shares.
